paragraphs.heading: When the sunspots vanished
paragraphs.text: The Maunder Minimum was a stretch from about 1645 to 1715 when sunspots almost disappeared. In the 28 years from 1672 to 1699, observers counted fewer than 50 of them. Over a similar span today, astronomers would expect to see 40,000 to 50,000.

paragraphs.heading: Who found it
paragraphs.text: Gustav Spörer first noticed the gap, in papers published in 1887 and 1889. His work was taken up and extended by the solar astronomers Edward Walter Maunder and his wife Annie Russell Maunder, who also tracked how the latitudes of sunspots changed over time. Two papers appeared under Edward's name alone, in 1890 and 1894. Annie had no university degree, and the rules of the day kept her share of the work from being publicly recognized. The name Maunder Minimum caught on after John A. Eddy published a landmark paper in Science in 1976.

paragraphs.heading: A dim, plain corona
paragraphs.text: Eddy also looked at eclipses of the Sun from this period. Working from written eyewitness accounts of the eclipses of 1652, 1706 and 1715, he decided the solar corona had been weak and had no clear structure. He had no pictures to check this against. In 2012, Markus Heinz of the Berlin State Library found two lost paintings of the 1706 eclipse by Maria Clara Eimmart, a skilled astronomer whose father directed an observatory in Nuremberg. They matched written descriptions of the same eclipse and confirmed Eddy's conclusion.

paragraphs.heading: The Little Ice Age question
paragraphs.text: The Maunder Minimum fell in the middle of the Little Ice Age, a long period from about 1300 to about 1850 when Europe and North America were colder than average. It is tempting to blame the quiet Sun, but whether one caused the other is still being studied. The cooling started well before the sunspots faded, and northern-hemisphere temperatures during the minimum were not much different from the previous 80 years. The leading explanation for the Little Ice Age is volcanic activity.

paragraphs.heading: Cold winters in some places
paragraphs.text: The Sun may still have shaped regional weather. A 2011 study linked low solar activity to the behaviour of the jet stream, giving milder winters in places such as southern Europe and Canada and colder ones in northern Europe and the United States. Measurements by NASA's Solar Radiation and Climate Experiment suggest the Sun's ultraviolet output varies more over the solar cycle than once thought, which may help explain links between few sunspots and cold English winters. Europe had some very harsh winters in this era, including 1683–84, 1694–95 and 1708–09.

paragraphs.heading: Clues stored on Earth
paragraphs.text: Records of the Sun's past activity also survive on Earth. Carbon-14 and beryllium-10, kept in places such as tree rings and ice sheets, act as stand-ins, or proxies, for solar activity, and they confirm it was low during the Maunder Minimum. Other quiet spells have been found, either by direct observation or from these isotopes, including the Spörer Minimum (1450–1540) and the less marked Dalton Minimum (1790–1820). There seem to have been 18 such minima in the last 8,000 years, and the Sun may spend up to a quarter of its time in them.
